title: cold-groove-priming-handoff-labnotes
body:
Purpose:
Quick internal scratchpad: experiment log for a small idea I called "cold groove priming" — try to reduce p99 spikes during cold cohorts by sequentially priming shards (hand-off) rather than priming everything at once. This is rough notes + numbers; not polished.

Background / motivation:
- We see p99 spikes when a subset of tenants hit cold after a deployment or after an autoscale; priming all contexts concurrently creates a microburst that contends for GPU and scheduler slots.
- Hypothesis: serializing priming across logical shards (a "groove" pattern) smooths the priming load and reduces p99 without increasing overall time-to-warm significantly.

Experiment design (quick):
1) Baseline: cold-start canonical priming (all shards concurrently).
2) Primed-serial: pick 4 logical shards, prime them sequentially with 3s gap.
3) Staggered-hand-off: start shard0->shard1->shard2 with overlap window 1s (small overlap to maintain throughput).

Traffic profile: synthetic k6 script (short pulses) approximating 80 qps overall across 4 shards; 30s pulse, 30s idle x 6.
Loadgen command (approx):
- k6 run --vus 40 --duration 00:06:00 --summary-export=out.json cold-groove.js
- probes instrumented via /metrics and tracing hooks (span tags: experiment, shard)

Environment:
- model: llama-2-7b quant8 variant (on dev dedicated pool)
- nodes: 2x A100-80GB, runtime build b2024.11.01
- scheduler: experimental preemptible slot aware  (feature-flag: prime-groove)

Raw numbers (extracted from summary traces, trimmed):
Run      | cohort       | qps | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | errors
Baseline  | all-concurrent | 80  | 34      | 220     | 930     | 0.45%
Primed-1  | serial-4x      | 80  | 36      | 88      | 160     | 0.05%
Staggered | overlap-1s     | 80  | 35      | 74      | 140     | 0.03%

Mini-interpretation:
- Baseline has acceptable p50/p95 but p99 ~ 930ms (very bad). Errors jump modestly during priming bursts.
- Serial priming (Primed-1) reduced p99 by ~5.8x vs baseline and reduced errors by ~9x. p95 also improved a lot.
- Staggered overlap gives slightly better p99 than pure serial; seems overlap window of ~1s trades off slightly higher p95 for lower p99.

ASCII p99 trend (R1->R3):
R1 [##########-------------------------] 930
R2 [###-------------------------------] 160
R3 [##--------------------------------] 140

Observations / signal checks:
- End-to-end tail improvements correlate with reduced concurrent GPU kernel queueing (checked via nvprof sample traces). In baseline there are many simultaneous kernel launches across contexts; serialization reduces simultaneous launches and KV-store contention.
- Memory pressure: small (~6%) additional resident memory for Primed-1 due to overlapping warm caches while staggered had slightly higher resident mem but still within headroom.
- Scheduling latency: scheduler traces show that concurrent priming causes scheduling jitter up to 120ms for small helper tasks; serialization brought this down <25ms.

Quick hypotheses for mechanism:
- GPU kernel queue saturation during mass priming causes stragglers; fewer concurrent priming flows reduces serialization and keeps latency-critical requests fast.
- KV cache write storms (when many priming flows populate shared cache shards) create lock contention in our in-memory cache + metrics emission overloads (promclient) which amplifies p99.

What I tried (commands / flags):
- prime-groove=true (scheduler) + groove-window=3000ms (serial)
- groove-overlap=1000ms (staggered)
- reduced priming batch-size from 64->32 to test if smaller batches alone help
- instrumentation: set tracing level to TRACE only for priming spans (avoid tracing full traffic)

Secondary micro-items (notes):
- Smaller priming batch-size helped p95 a bit but did not address p99 as well as groove. Suggests admission shaping is needed + groove.
- Need to sanity-check long-tail for larger payloads (2x length) and with real client mix (not k6).

Open questions / TODOs:
- Re-run with three different groove-window sizes (1s, 3s, 6s) and measure time-to-full-warm vs p99. Capture cost tradeoffs (extra seconds of reduced throughput per tenant).
- Run with real traffic replay (shadow traffic) to validate. I have a recording ticket: INF-2398 (linked) — TODO: schedule shadow run next week.
- Explore hybrid: dynamic groove-window based on current scheduler queue length metric.

Quick conclusions (for now):
- Serializing priming (cold groove) is a low-risk mitigation that materially reduces tail latency induced by cold cohorts.
- Staggered (small overlap) gives slightly better overall tradeoff than pure serial in our microbench.
- Next step: automate groove-window selection and test with multi-model mix.

Notes-to-self:
- Save nvprof slices for R1-R3 under /tmp/fernanda/cold-groove/ (already pulled).
- Make small PR to add prime-groove feature flag telemetry (counts, window, overlap) so we can correlate in prod-run.

References and quick links:
- PR with scheduler changes: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/482
- Ticket: INF-2376 (priming smoothing experiments)

End.
